correction_1.truth: it is the GENERATION GUARD's expected-value materialization; direct exits are patched, so the movz/movk stub holding that chain is dead code

correction_2.claim_struck: the guard's ldar cost is acquire ordering (or a D-cache miss on the generation cell)
correction_2.truth: REFUTED by experiment. Generation cells are L1-resident (166 lines = 10.6 KB vs 64 KB L1D). A store-count ladder holding the guard fixed shows ldar, ldapr and plain ldr all cost the same as NO LOAD AT ALL; cost tracks context-STORE count only
correction_2.consequence: the block prologue is STORE-THROUGHPUT-BOUND. The guard's load is where retirement stalls waiting on the store queue, so the drain skids onto it; the five entry stores are the cause

chaining_verdict: UNSOUND and worse than previously recorded: link severing does not exist anywhere in the tree (PublishedBlock retains no links, so there is no reverse index), and trusted entry would degrade the guard from per-block to per-gateway-entry, leaving a self-linked hot loop generation-checked once for its whole lifetime
chaining_salvage: superblock formation IS sound and needs no new safety story: one AssembledBlock means internal edges are dynasm labels, not patched slots, so there is nothing to sever and one guard covers the unit. HARD CONSTRAINT: must not cross a guest page boundary, because the guard is single-page and `sensitive` metadata is keyed (guest_pc, block_generation)
implication: optimize the block prologue by removing STORES, not by tuning the guard's load or its comparison

refuses to swallow a fused exclusive region as a continuation; that emitter owns its whole block
superblocks are excluded from the artifact and shared-translation caches, whose templates are keyed on one block's source words -- a lost cache hit, never wrong code

question: are the workload's page faults driven by carrick's codegen?
answer: essentially NO. 2.08% of zero-fill faults are JIT first-touch; 1.48% are inserted code. Faults are dominated by the guest's own anonymous memory.

finding: the EMITTED ranking differs sharply from the EXECUTED ranking, and it promotes one lever: dsr:x17-materialize is 29.1% of all emitted words -- the largest single class, larger than any guest class -- against 13.9% of sampled executed PCs. Exit-target materialization dominates footprint far more than cycles. The design doc's Phase C already names the fix (load the target from the context or a literal pool instead of a four-word movz/movk chain, as `26de3c07` already did for gateway addresses), and it would cut both footprint and cycles.
corrected: an earlier estimate of 4.1 GB emitted / 14.3% of zfod faults was wrong by 5.1x. `cache_used_bytes` is a PER-THREAD profile frame; summing the frames counts each process's cache once per thread (444 frames, 68 processes). Correct by-pid sum is 812,782,912 bytes and the directly measured snapshot total is 599,208,872.
method_rule: third aggregation error of this campaign, all the same shape: rank or sum without establishing the denominator. Print the total and the top entry's share of it; never sum a per-thread gauge as a per-process quantity.
tool: scripts/perf/emitted_shape.py (reuses shape_classify.classify verbatim so both views bucket identically)

method: scripts/dtrace/native-whole-cpu-budget.d, one cold go-build. profile-997 over the tracked tree, so samples/997 IS aggregate CPU-seconds -- the denominator every share is quoted against. Tracking is by carrick's own lifecycle USDT under `dtrace -Z` (`carrick*:::dsr-cache-capacity`), NOT by execname: execname is the binary basename and silently tracks nothing when the binary is renamed, which is what happens when comparing two built arms.
finding: Codegen is NOT the biggest bucket. DSR-inserted words are 18.6% of total CPU, not the ~30-40% the earlier census implied. The two largest buckets are user code OUTSIDE the JIT (36.9% -- carrick's own host text plus dylibs) and kernel time in NO syscall or mach trap (25.7% -- page-fault handling, with 1.71M zero-fill and 2.11M address-space faults). Together 62.6%. Guest instructions are 8.5% (3.51 CPU-s), which cross-checks against Docker's ~2.26 CPU-s for the same work.
bounds: 58% of user samples fell outside the JIT snapshots, so the 36.9% cannot be split between carrick host text, dylibs and non-JIT guest code from this run alone; the earlier range-classifier census split that population 16.8%/14.7%, implying carrick host ~20% and dylibs ~17%. The syscall on-CPU total varies run to run (4.12, 5.57, 6.12 CPU-s across three traced runs) because vtimestamp accounting is itself perturbed by tracing, so treat the syscall share as the softest number here and the sample-based splits as the firm ones.
consequence: Rank the next work off this table, not off the emitted-word census. Page-fault handling and carrick's host-side userspace are each larger than all inserted codegen, and neither has been attacked.
